title: The German words hiding in English

entries.note: From German, literally a double walker or double-goer; first meant a ghostly apparition of a living person in English, and meeting yours supposedly means you'll perish.
From German, literally a noisy ghost; its geist, ghost or spirit, also appears in [[see:zeitgeist]].
Given as an example of the dialects of German still spoken in America.
Said after sneezes in America and, almost militantly, in Germany; means healthiness, and gesund is related to English [[same-root:sound]]; Britons say [[equivalent:bless you]].
What Britons say after a sneeze instead of [[equivalent:Gesundheit]].
In the sense healthy or safe, related to the gesund of [[same-root:Gesundheit]], conveniently since a sneeze is a loud sound.
Prefix that turns a verb into a noun, as in [[see:Getränk]]; Old English had it too, usually with a y sound, but English has largely dropped it.
German for a drink, formed by putting [[see:ge-]] in front of the verb.
The branch English belongs to along with German, Dutch, Flemish and Low German, making English and German sibling languages.
Rob thinks a German might understand it better than a modern English speaker, given its three genders and German-like case system.
Consistent consonant changes that split High German from other West Germanic languages, popularised by [[see:Jacob Grimm]]; Rob's video shows how knowing it helps translate German.
Example of German d matching English th under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of German d matching English th under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of German d matching English th under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of German d matching English th under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of English t corresponding to German s under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of English t corresponding to German s under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
A double example of English p becoming an f sound in German under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
A double example of English p becoming an f sound in German under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of English p matching a German f sound under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of English p matching a German f sound under the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]].
Example of English w or y sounds corresponding to German g.
Combines two correspondences: English y sound to German g, and English d to German t.

entries.translation: beef labelling supervision duties delegation law
entries.note: A real meat-labelling law in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania from 1999 to 2013, which breaks down into simple elements: beef meat, labelling, supervision, duties, delegation law.
Glossed as a German state when introducing the meat-labelling law [[see:Rindfleischetikettierungsüberwachungsaufgabenübertragungsgesetz]].
Job title its holders could theoretically have used from 1829 to 1991; Donau is Danube, Dampfschiff steamboat, Fahrt journey, Gesellschaft society, Kapitän captain.
A famous Berlin department store, short for Kaufhaus des Westens; it takes the first letters of each element, a popular German way to form brand names.
Short for Albrecht Discount, formed from the opening letters of each element.
Discussed before; formed from the name Adi Dassler, the same principle as [[see:Aldi]], though it is not an acronym.
Short for German [[from:Fliegerabwehrkanone]], aircraft defence cannon; entered English in 1938 for an anti-aircraft gun, and by the 1940s meant the exploding fire itself.
Comes from the shrapnel damage of anti-aircraft [[from:flak]] fire.
From WWI German substitute products like acorn coffee made under the Allied blockade; German just means replacement, but English implies fake or inferior.
Probably not used in English before the Second World War; from [[from:blitzkrieg]], lightning war.
From German for broken.
Language of the Ashkenazi Jews, many in New York, a form of High German through which English probably got [[see:shvitz]] and [[see:mensch]].
German for sweat, though English speakers probably took it from [[from:Yiddish]] rather than German.
German for person, probably borrowed via [[from:Yiddish]]; used kindly in English, as in a real mensch.
Jess wonders whether it boosted [[see:mensch]]; originally Nietzsche's idea, later associated with the Nazis.
Another word English has borrowed from German.
An era's intellectual or cultural climate; coined by [[see:Johann Gottfried Herder]] in the 1760s, brought into English by [[see:Thomas Carlyle]]; Zeit is cognate with [[same-root:tide]].
Cognate with [[same-root:tide]], as is the Zeit of [[see:zeitgeist]].
Cognate with the Zeit of [[same-root:zeitgeist]], showing German ts for English t.
Simply German for fear, but in English it carries an existential element it lacks in German.
A psychology term for the combined whole of something, from German for shape or form, used more haughtily in English.
Deep weariness at the gap between the world as it is and as it ought to be; its Schmerz is the same word as English [[same-root:smart]].
Arguably now part of English and used constantly; an example of German's knack for naming emotions English lacks words for.
Feeling someone else's joy.
Feeling someone else's shame on their behalf.
Borrowed from German; English has the same elements, though English [[see:lust]] differs from the German sense; connected with [[see:Wanderschaft]].
Freud's term, translated into English as the pleasure principle, showing German Lust is broader than English [[see:lust]].
English lust is largely sexual, whereas German Lust is general desire, as in [[see:Lust auf Tee]].
Example of the non-sexual German sense of [[see:lust]]: simply fancying a tea.
The traditional journeying period for journeymen, from German Romanticism and connected with [[see:wanderlust]]; its ending is [[see:-schaft]].
The ending of [[see:Wanderschaft]], equivalent to English -ship.
In the sense of hurting, the same word as the Schmerz of [[same-root:Weltschmerz]].
German for black, matching Old English [[same-root:swart]].
Old and Middle English word for black alongside black, the two naming different blacks, shiny versus deep-hole dark; survives in [[gave:swarthy]].
Survival of [[from:swart]]; now feels like an antiquated, even racist, insult from Victorian novels and Heathcliff, perhaps with a piratey tone.
Not itself a loan word but a [[see:calque]] of German [[from:Lehnwort]]; otherwise English would simply say Lehnwort.
Translating a word's elements rather than borrowing it; French for copy, from calquer, to trace by rubbing, itself from Italian, possibly related to [[same-root?:chalk]].
Example of a straightforward borrowing, in contrast to a [[see:calque]].
Rob guesses it is related to [[same-root?:calque]], as in a chalk rubbing.
Of the fairy-tale Brothers Grimm, who collected tales to analyse language; popularised the [[see:second Germanic consonant shift]] and made [[see:ablaut]] a technical term.
Indo-European vowel alternation, as in sing, sang, sung, song or ride, rode, ridden; English got it via [[see:Franz Bopp]], and [[see:Jacob Grimm]] made it technical in 1819.
Vowel fronting caused by a lost i in an ending (man/men, foot/feet), and the German two dots marking it; laut is related to [[same-root:loud]].
Related to the laut of [[same-root:umlaut]] and the Lud of [[same-root:Ludwig]].
English name for [[see:umlaut]], so called because a lost i sound in an ending reshaped the preceding vowel.
The French two dots, which separate two vowel sounds rather than altering the vowel as the German [[see:umlaut]] does.
German for king; surnames like Koenig write oe instead of the [[see:umlaut]].
Surname anglicised without the [[see:umlaut]]; schön means beautiful and Berg mountain, so perhaps someone from a place called Schönberg.
A word basically the same in many languages, like chai or tea, ginger, copper, silver, mint or honey, usually for something traded.
A recurring musical phrase, also usable in literature, associated with Wagnerian music drama, though Mozart used them too.
A [[equivalent:coming of age story]]; a mix of German and French, its second part tied to [[see:romance]].
The plain English equivalent of [[equivalent:Bildungsroman]].
First a work written in French; as these featured kings, knights and love, Germanic languages applied it to any courtly adventure story, then to courtly love.
A place where children flourish like flowers, founded by [[see:Friedrich Fröbel]]; the generic American word for preschool, but rare in Britain, which says [[equivalent:nursery school]].
The usual British term, rather than [[equivalent:kindergarten]].
Inventor of the [[see:kindergarten]], born 1782, who lost his mother as a baby and fought Napoleon; Prussia banned his kindergartens, so teachers fled abroad.
Founded the first English-language [[see:kindergarten]] in Boston in 1860, after a German-language one in Watertown, Wisconsin, in 1856.
Simple toys like blocks or a ball given to [[see:kindergarten]] children so their imagination could run free.
Its Ruck is related to English [[same-root:ridge]], ultimately from the Old English word for back.
Spelled hrycg in Old English and ultimately a word for the back; related to the Ruck of [[same-root:rucksack]].
From [[from:knappen]], to eat, literally to crack or snap; Germans pronounce the K.
Originally a bag for oats, like a horse's oat bag; German Hafer is oat, as in [[same-root:Hafermilch]].
A sausage from an earlier episode, recalled because Germans pronounce its initial K, as in [[see:knapsack]].
German for oat milk, sharing the Hafer of [[same-root:haversack]].
Swiss German with the cute diminutive [[see:-li]]; Mus is related to [[same-root:mush]]; in England a specific oat-and-fruit cereal, in Germany breakfast cereals broadly.
Regional Swiss German diminutive suffix making things cute, as in [[see:muesli]]; compare [[see:-lein]] and [[see:-chen]].
German diminutive meaning little one, compared with [[see:-li]].
German diminutive meaning little, compared with [[see:-li]].
Related to the Mus of [[same-root:muesli]], though less cute.
Jess likens [[see:muesli]] to less sugary granola, prompting the joke 'misery granola'.
Means fart goblin or fart devil; its nickel is the metal's [[same-root:nickel]], since Nicholas was associated with goblins and the devil, as in [[see:Old Nick]].
The metal's name contains the same nickel as [[same-root:pumpernickel]].
English name for the devil, reflecting the link between Nicholas and goblins behind [[see:pumpernickel]].
Thought of as quintessentially American but just means thing from Hamburg; through rebracketing, every [[gave:burger]] is named after Hamburg.
The thing from Frankfurt.
The thing from Vienna.
A rebracketing of [[from:hamburger]], so even a [[see:beef burger]] or [[see:cheeseburger]] is named after Hamburg.
Still named after Hamburg; Rob grew up thinking it differed from a [[see:hamburger]] because shops like Iceland sold beef burgers.
Also ultimately named after Hamburg via [[from:burger]].
A very literal German description: sour cabbage.
Means a cut, from [[from:schneiden]], to cut.
Borrowed from German though not associated with Germany; possibly related to [[same-root?:Knödel]] and [[same-root?:knot]]; German Nudel means any pasta.
Possibly related to [[same-root?:noodle]] through a word for dumpling.
A kind of dumpling, one of several doughy words possibly related to [[same-root?:noodle]].
Both word and concept came from German, thanks to [[see:Haribo]], whose German packet calls them [[see:Goldbären]].
Brand name from the first syllables of [[from:Hans Riegel]], its founder, and Bonn, where he founded it.
The name on the German packet of [[see:Haribo]] [[see:gummy bear]]s.
Best theory: from an unattested Latin [[from?:bracchiatellum]], folded arms, linking it to [[same-root?:brachiosaurus]]; Rob plans a short about it.
Literally arm lizard, possibly sharing an arm root with [[same-root?:pretzel]].
Bred by [[see:Max von Stephanitz]], who standardised German herding dogs, favouring wolflike, pointy-eared, intelligent, hardworking ones; also called [[see:Alsatian]].
Name for the [[see:German Shepherd]] adopted because the British avoided saying German in WWI; the dog isn't from [[see:Alsace]].
Region that repeatedly changed hands between Germany and France, where Alsatian, a form of High German, is spoken.
Called [[see:Deutsche Dogge]], German dog, in German, which is confusing.
German name for the [[see:Great Dane]], using a borrowing of English [[from:dog]], which other languages apply to big dogs like mastiffs.
Discussed before as having no relatives in other languages, so their versions are borrowings, used for big breeds like [[see:mastiff]]s.
The kind of big dog other languages call by English [[see:dog]].
Basically a puddle dog, meaning a water dog.
Snarler or growler, from a word for snout or muzzle, as in [[see:Berliner Schnauze]].
The grumpy attitude Berliners are criticised for; Schnauze is the snout of [[see:schnauzer]].
Thing from Rottweil, whose weil is like Latin [[same-root:villa]], farm, and rot maybe red; shortened from [[from:Rottweil butcher's dog]].
In Latin a farm rather than a house, compared with the weil of [[same-root:Rottweiler]].
Original name of the [[gave:Rottweiler]], used to guard livestock, drive cattle and pull carts of meat.
From [[from:Joachimsthaler]], big coins minted in the Joachimsthal valley, shortened to Thaler and eventually dollar; probably covered in their money episode.
Comes from the Neander Valley.
Discussed before; a badger hound, because they went down badger holes after badgers.
Named after the breeder [[from:Karl Friedrich Louis Dobermann]].
A word for a terrier-type dog, related to [[same-root:pinch]] for its little nipping.
Related to [[same-root:pinscher]], from the dogs' nipping.
Named after [[from:Rudolf Diesel]], who developed it.
Named after [[from:Ferdinand von Zeppelin]].
Named after [[from:Robert Bunsen]].
Named after [[from:Hans Geiger]].
Named after [[from:Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit]].
Named after [[from:Heinrich Hertz]].
Named after the Austrian physicist [[from:Christian Doppler]].
Named after [[from:August Ferdinand Möbius]].
From [[from:Franz Anton Mesmer]], proponent of animal magnetism and hypnotism, whose name charlatans used for ideas he didn't hold.
Means famous in war; its Lud is related to [[same-root:loud]].
Means war struggle, or struggle struggle.
Means battle; related to [[same-root:Hildebrand]], and the element also appears in [[same-root:Matilda]].
Its brand is related to [[same-root:brandish]] and [[same-root:brand]], from a root meaning burning, perhaps from swords flashing.
Related to the brand of [[same-root:Hildebrand]].
Related to [[same-root:Hildebrand]] through a root meaning burning; German Brand still means fire, as in a house fire.
Means battle-ready in armour, or armour battle.
Means mighty in battle, containing the hild of [[same-root:Hilda]].
Old English for battle, used in many a [[see:kenning]], like [[see:hildbedd]].
A [[see:kenning]] meaning deathbed.
A [[see:kenning]] for blood dripping from a sword, evoking cold steel.
A [[see:kenning]] for an arrow, lance or spear.
Poetic metaphorical compounds, like the Old English [[see:hild]] terms, that don't necessarily stick around.
Weary of fighting; its [[see:sad]] has the old sense of satiated or fed up.
In [[see:hildesæd]] it means fed up or satiated, like German satt.
Means noble bright.
Means noble bright, like [[see:Albert]].
Means the bright one.
Originally German, meaning bold as a bear, with versions in various languages.
Rob's name; its -bert means bright in German and also in Old English, since the languages were closely related.
Means fun, though it doesn't sound like it.
